attempts.label: DRYAD:4j0zpc8hz
attempts.entry_title: Chronic warming and dry soils in beech and oak (Didion-Gency et al. 2024)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Didion-Gency, Vitasse, Buchmann, Gessler, Gisler, Schaub and Grossiord (2024) on Dryad dataset 4j0zpc8hz, one table of 96 beech and oak trees grown in open-top chambers under warming and soil moisture reduction, in monocultures and mixtures, from 2019 to 2021. It tests the phenology regressions on air temperature, the treatment effects on leaf water potential, carbon relations and growth, and the effects of species mixture. The soil moisture and chamber climate records are not in the dataset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Didion-Gency et al. (2024) from Dryad dataset 4j0zpc8hz

outcomes.statement: Warmer spring air advanced bud swelling in both species, by 1.1 days per degree in beech and 2.3 days per degree in oak, across 2020 and 2021 and the four treatments.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1A and 1B
outcomes.quote: Higher daily air temperatures in spring were linked to an earlier bud swelling in both species, where beech was advanced by −1.1 d °C−1 and oak by −2.3 d °C−1 across the 2 yr and treatments

statistics.n: monoculture trees, 6 per treatment, species and year, 2020 and 2021

outcomes.notes: Slopes of bud swelling on Tspring, monoculture trees 2020 and 2021, -1.078 days per degree in beech and -2.296 in oak, both within tolerance; P1 p = 0.00011 and 1.2e-08, P2 (8 treatment-year means) p = 0.033 and 0.010. The slopes are equal under P1 and P2 because every treatment-year has six trees. With a random intercept per treatment and year added to P1 (a variant, not a reading of the claims file), p = 0.0060 and 0.0002.
deviations: Reading P1 uses each tree-year against its treatment's temperature, as the dataset gives one temperature per treatment and year and no chamber value.
The sensor height (H1, 50 cm, or H2, 2 m) of the deposited temperatures is not stated, so H1 and H2 could not be run separately.

outcomes.statement: Warmer spring air shortened leaf development duration by 0.7 days per degree in both species.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1C and 1D
outcomes.quote: A shorter leaf development duration was also found, with a reduction of −0.7 d °C−1 in both species
outcomes.notes: Slopes of development duration on Tspring, -0.651 (beech) and -0.659 (oak) days per degree, within 0.7 +- 0.07. Under P1 p = 0.0010 and 0.0039; under P2 the oak regression has p = 0.16, so only P1 meets the criterion, which needs one reading. P1 treats the 48 tree-years as independent although the temperature is one value per treatment and year; with a random intercept per treatment and year (a variant, not a reading of the claims file), oak has p = 0.11 and beech 0.012, so the oak result rests on P1 as the claims file gives it.
deviations: Reading P1 uses each tree-year against its treatment's temperature, as the dataset gives one temperature per treatment and year and no chamber value.
The sensor height (H1, 50 cm, or H2, 2 m) of the deposited temperatures is not stated, so H1 and H2 could not be run separately.

outcomes.statement: Warmer fall air extended leaf senescence duration by 3.4 days per degree in beech and 3.1 days per degree in oak.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1G and 1H
outcomes.quote: Similarly, senescence duration was extended by +3.4 d °C−1 in beech and +3.1 d °C−1 in oak
outcomes.notes: Slopes of senescence duration on Tfall, 3.396 (beech) and 3.084 (oak) days per degree, within tolerance; p <= 0.0056 under P1 and P2, and p < 0.0001 with a random intercept per treatment and year (a variant).
deviations: Reading P1 uses each tree-year against its treatment's temperature, as the dataset gives one temperature per treatment and year and no chamber value.
The sensor height (H1, 50 cm, or H2, 2 m) of the deposited temperatures is not stated, so H1 and H2 could not be run separately.

outcomes.statement: Warmer annual air lengthened the growing season by 4.5 days per degree in beech and 5.7 days per degree in oak.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1I and 1J
outcomes.quote: The growing seasons were extended by +4.5 d °C−1 and +5.7 d °C−1 for beech and oak, respectively, with an increase in daily mean annual air temperature
outcomes.notes: Slopes of the deposited growing season length on Tannual, 4.460 (beech) and 5.652 (oak) days per degree, within tolerance; p <= 0.035 under P1 and P2. The deposited Growth_length never equals onset of senescence minus bud swelling, the Methods' definition (median difference 55 days); with that definition, which the criterion repeats (bud swelling to onset of senescence), the slopes are 1.09 (beech, P1 p = 0.085) and 2.16 (oak, P1 p = 0.0014), and the claim would not be reproduced. Neither the workbook nor Metadata.csv defines Growth_length. The outcome uses the deposited column, which gives the paper's slopes within 0.04; a question asks which is to be tested. With a random intercept per treatment and year (a variant), p = 0.0067 and < 0.0001.
deviations: Reading P1 uses each tree-year against its treatment's temperature, as the dataset gives one temperature per treatment and year and no chamber value.
The sensor height (H1, 50 cm, or H2, 2 m) of the deposited temperatures is not stated, so H1 and H2 could not be run separately.
The deposited Growth_length is used; it does not follow the Methods' definition (see findings).

outcomes.statement: The temperature-driven advance was larger in oak than in beech (P = 0.004, least squares analysis).
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: However chronic warming was more advantageous to oak than to beech as the advancement of bud swelling extension was higher in oak (P = 0.004 using Least-squares analysis)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), bud swelling on Tspring by species, each tree-year (P1): oak slope -2.30 against beech -1.08, species by temperature interaction p = 0.0046 (paper 0.004). On treatment means (P2) p = 0.12; reading (b), growing season length on Tannual, p = 0.36 (P1) and 0.57 (P2), oak slope 5.65 against 4.46. With a random intercept per species, treatment and year added to P1 (a variant, not a reading of the claims file), reading (a) gives p = 0.097, so the result rests on P1 as the claims file gives it.
deviations: Reading P1 uses each tree-year against its treatment's temperature, as the dataset gives one temperature per treatment and year and no chamber value.
The sensor height (H1, 50 cm, or H2, 2 m) of the deposited temperatures is not stated, so H1 and H2 could not be run separately.

outcomes.statement: The onset of senescence was not related to fall air temperature in either species.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Figure 1E and 1F
outcomes.quote: No relationship between the onset of senescence and fall daily air temperatures was found, suggesting that the onset of senescence is not driven by temperature changes in the fall for both species
outcomes.notes: No regression of onset of senescence on Tfall has P <= 0.05 (p 0.44 to 0.80 over species and P1, P2); slopes 0.24 (beech) and -0.45 (oak) days per degree; p 0.79 and 0.45 with a random intercept per treatment and year (a variant). 48 of 191 tree-years have an onset at day 250 to 252, the start of the observations.
deviations: Reading P1 uses each tree-year against its treatment's temperature, as the dataset gives one temperature per treatment and year and no chamber value.
The sensor height (H1, 50 cm, or H2, 2 m) of the deposited temperatures is not stated, so H1 and H2 could not be run separately.

outcomes.statement: No phenological trait was related to soil moisture in either species.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 1; Supplemental Figure S1
outcomes.quote: We observed no significant relationship between phenology and soil moisture for both species (Supplemental Fig. S1)
outcomes.notes: The dataset has no soil moisture (Mspring, Mfall, Mannual or the 25 cm records); the workbook and Metadata.csv list every column and none is a soil moisture variable. The paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: The more chilling days trees received, the fewer growing degree days they needed to reach bud swelling, in both species, following a negative exponential.
outcomes.source: Results, Phenology, paragraph 2; Figure 2A and 2B
outcomes.quote: With an increase in the number of chilling days, both species had lower GDD requirements to budburst (Fig. 2)

statistics.n: monoculture trees, one point per tree and year, 2020 and 2021

outcomes.notes: With the deposited GDD and Chill_days, monoculture trees 2020 and 2021 (48 per species), both forms of the negative exponential decrease over the observed range in both species. (e) GDD = a exp(b CD): b = -0.0135 (beech, p = 4.4e-27, R2 0.95), -0.0114 (oak, p = 7.4e-20, R2 0.88). (f) GDD = a + b exp(c CD): c = -0.035 (beech, p = 2.9e-07), -0.054 (oak, p = 4.2e-07).
deviations: The readings (a) or (b) for GDD, (c) or (d) for the end of the chilling count, and H1 or H2 could not be run separately: the dataset gives GDD and chilling days already computed and not the temperature records. Metadata.csv says chilling days run to leaf flushing (reading d).

outcomes.statement: Even without warming, trees received at most 97 chilling days.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 1; Figure 2

outcomes.notes: Largest Chill_days among C and MR monoculture trees in 2020 and 2021 is 97 (2021; 82 and 76 in 2020); 97 is also the largest in the dataset.
deviations: Chilling days are the deposited values; readings (c), (d), H1 and H2 could not be run separately.

findings.statement: Metadata.csv and the README sheet give the treatment codes as C, W, MR and WMR; the Treatment column holds C, D, H and HD. The Warming and Soil moisture reduction columns map them one to one (H is W, D is MR, HD is WMR).

The 'Total Data' sheet has 35 rows that repeat another row exactly (trees 17, 35, 45 and 144; tree 35 has 24 rows in place of 9), and tree 144 has two rows for campaign 5 of 2020 with different sugar (7.71 and 6.69 %) and starch (4.99 and 9.99 %) values.

Starch (77 tree-campaign rows, down to -6.28 %), sugar (3, down to -4.06 %) and Asat (5, down to -0.29) have negative values, which a concentration or a light-saturated assimilation rate cannot have; the paper takes their square root.

Growth_length ('growing season length') never equals onset of senescence minus bud swelling (Senes_10 - Flush_S1), the Methods' definition: it is a median 55 days longer, and 2 to 33 days longer than the end of senescence (Senes_10 + Senes_time) minus bud swelling. Its definition is not given.
Diameter_growth is labelled cm, but its values (median 0.42, up to 4.46 a year) on stems of 5.2 to 6.1 mm at planting (Table S4) are consistent with mm.

The soil moisture (Mspring, Mfall, Mannual), the chamber climate records (air temperature, relative humidity, VPD, soil temperature and water content at 10 min) and the initial heights and diameters (Table S4) are not deposited; five claims rest on them.

Tspring, Tfall and Tannual are one value per treatment and year (the same in the four chambers of a treatment), and the sensor height (50 cm or 2 m) they come from is not stated; GDD and Chill_days are given per tree without the records they were computed from, and the GDD description does not say whether the excess over 5 C or the daily mean is summed.
Four compartments (6 in chambers A3, A4, B3 and B4) hold a beech monoculture tree and an oak mixture tree, which the design (a compartment holds a monoculture or a mixture) does not allow.
AGB_growth (estimated AGWB increment) is exactly 0 in 57 of 191 tree-years of 2020 and 2021, whose median height increment is 5 cm, and is never negative; how it was bounded is not described.

Refitting the paper's treatment model on the dataset with marginal F tests gives Supplemental Table S1's F values for oak AGWB increment exactly and for beech Asat within 0.25, which links the deposited table to the paper's analysis; other traits match less closely.

The Methods say the treatments started in June 2019, after the first leaf flushing and measurement campaign, and that 2019 is not included in the study, yet the treatment model has year 2019 to 2021 as a fixed effect (Table S1's F and p pairs for terms with year fit two numerator df, as the claims file notes). Under reading T1, which follows that model, the 2019 yearly means (L1) and the 2019 campaign values (L2) include the first campaign, measured before the treatments began.

entries.name: dryad-4j0zpc8hz-didion-gency-2024
entries.title: Chronic warming and dry soils in beech and oak (Didion-Gency et al. 2024)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Didion-Gency, Vitasse, Buchmann, Gessler, Gisler, Schaub and Grossiord (2024) on Dryad dataset 4j0zpc8hz, one table of 96 beech and oak trees grown in open-top chambers under warming and soil moisture reduction, in monocultures and mixtures, from 2019 to 2021. It tests the phenology regressions on air temperature, the treatment effects on leaf water potential, carbon relations and growth, and the effects of species mixture. The soil moisture and chamber climate records are not in the dataset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Didion-Gency et al. (2024) from Dryad dataset 4j0zpc8hz
